title: 2 Kings 17:7–18
context: The narrator pauses to explain the exile theologically. Israel had forgotten the God who brought them out of Egypt, adopted the practices of the nations, built high places, worshiped idols and the heavenly bodies, served Baal, and even made their children pass through the fire. The LORD had warned them through every prophet, but they hardened their necks, so he removed them from his sight.

verses.text: It was so because the children of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator explains that this happened because Israel sinned against the God who brought them out of Egypt. Arminian readers stress that the exile responds to a freely chosen and persistent rejection of a gracious Redeemer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the indictment begins with grace: the God of the exodus. Sin is ingratitude toward the one who redeemed them, which makes the judgment all the more just. How the traditions read such covenant conditions is treated in the Leviticus 26:3 box.

verses.text: and walked in the statutes of the nations whom the LORD cast out from before the children of Israel, and of the kings of Israel, which they made.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel walked in the customs of the nations and the practices their own kings introduced. Arminian readers note that both popular culture and royal policy shaped the people, yet each generation remained responsible for following them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Israel became like the nations the LORD had driven out, reversing the purpose of the conquest. The people God set apart chose to blend in.

verses.text: The children of Israel secretly did things that were not right against the LORD their God; and they built high places for themselves in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified city;
verses.arminianNotes: Israel secretly did what was not right and built high places everywhere, from watchtower to fortified city. Arminian readers note the hidden nature of the sin, a reminder that God sees what people try to conceal.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase from watchtower to fortified city suggests every kind of settlement, small and large. Reformed readers see sin spreading through the whole land, so that no place remained untouched.

verses.text: and they set up for themselves pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree;
verses.arminianNotes: Pillars and Asherah poles stood on every hill and under every green tree. Arminian readers see how idolatry became woven into the landscape, normalized by repetition until it seemed ordinary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase echoes the commands of Deuteronomy 12:2-3, where Israel was told to destroy such places. Israel instead multiplied what it had been commanded to remove.

verses.text: and there they burned incense in all the high places, as the nations whom the LORD carried away before them did; and they did wicked things to provoke the LORD to anger;
verses.arminianNotes: They burned incense on the high places as the nations had done, provoking the LORD. Arminian readers stress that Israel knowingly imitated practices that had led to the nations’ removal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an irony: Israel repeats the sins for which the Canaanites lost the land, and so loses the land in turn. God’s judgment is consistent.

verses.text: and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, “You shall not do this thing.”
verses.arminianNotes: They served idols despite the LORD’s clear command, You shall not do this thing. Arminian readers note that the command was plain, so the disobedience was deliberate rather than mistaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the clarity of God’s word leaving Israel without excuse. The problem was not ignorance but a heart turned away from what it knew.

verses.text: Yet the LORD testified to Israel and to Judah, by every prophet and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and seer, calling them to turn. Arminian readers see God’s sincere desire for repentance and a real opportunity to respond, as discussed in the Deuteronomy 5:29 box.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize God’s patience in sending prophet after prophet. The warnings were real and gracious, and the people’s refusal was their own; Reformed readers also see the warnings as means God uses in his purposes.

verses.text: Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck like the neck of their fathers who didn’t believe in the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: They would not listen but hardened their neck like their fathers. Arminian readers see self-hardening as a free and culpable response, a pattern repeated across generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stiff neck recalls Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 32:9). The Psalms 78:8 box already discusses how the traditions read a stubborn generation, and its discussion applies here.

verses.text: They rejected his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers, and his testimonies which he testified to them; and they followed vanity, and became vain, and followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them.
verses.arminianNotes: They rejected God’s statutes and covenant, followed vanity, and became vain. Arminian readers see how people come to resemble what they pursue, a sober warning about the formative power of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often connect the phrase followed vanity and became vain with Psalm 115:8 and Romans 1:21, where idolaters become like the empty things they serve.

verses.text: They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made molten images for themselves, even two calves, and made an Asherah, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served Baal.
verses.arminianNotes: They made two calves, an Asherah, worshiped the army of the sky, and served Baal. Arminian readers note the accumulation of false worship, each step building on earlier compromise.
verses.reformedNotes: The two calves go back to Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28), and worship of the heavenly bodies was forbidden in Deuteronomy 4:19. Reformed readers see the full catalog as the culmination of centuries of departure.

verses.text: They caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, to provoke him to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: They made their sons and daughters pass through the fire, practiced divination, and sold themselves to evil. Arminian readers state plainly that child sacrifice, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10, was among the gravest of Israel’s sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the words sold themselves describes slavery to sin chosen by the people themselves. Offering children to false gods marks the depth of corruption that idolatry produced.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight. There was none left but the tribe of Judah only.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD was very angry and removed Israel from his sight, leaving only Judah. Arminian readers read divine anger as God’s just and personal response to persistent covenant betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read God’s anger as holy and just, not capricious. The 1 Samuel 12:22 box already addresses how God’s commitment to his people relates to judgment on a particular generation.
